§ 3Metals and Non-Metals

METALS

  • They are generally solids.
  • Exception: Mercury (Hg) is liquid in room temperature, while Caesium (Cs) and Gallium (Ga) have melting points just above room temperature (28.5°C and 30°C, respectively).
  • They have a metallic lustre (shine).
  • Exception: Lead (Pb).
  • They are generally hard.
  • Exception: Alkali metals like Lithium, Sodium, and Potassium are soft metals and can be cut with a knife.
  • They have high melting point and boiling point.
  • Exception: Gallium (Ga) and Caesium (Cs).
  • They are malleable in nature (gold (Au) and silver (Ag) are most malleable metals). E.g. Sweets coated with thin sheets of Ag foil.
  • Exception: Mercury (Hg → liquid), Na (soft), K (soft), Zn (brittle).
  • They are ductile in nature (Au is most ductile).
  • Exception: Hg, Na, K, Zn.
  • They are sonorous in nature. They make or produce sound. E.g. School bells, temple bells, etc.
  • They have high density. Osmium has the highest density.
  • Exception: Sodium (Na) and Potassium (K) float in water.
  • They form alloys by combining with other metals or non-metals. E.g. Stainless steel alloy of Nickel (Ni), Chromium (Cr), and Iron (Fe). German silver, also known as "Nickel silver" is an alloy of Copper (Cu), Zinc (Zn) and Nickel (Ni).
  • Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity (free electrons are required for conduction of electricity).
  • Exception: Pb and Hg.
  • They exhibit cationic properties.
  • Metals form metal oxides when they react with oxygen. Generally, all metallic oxides are basic in nature.

NON-METALS

  • They are generally solids or gases.
  • Exception: Bromine (liquid at room temperature).
  • They are non-lustrous in nature.
  • Exception: Iodine, Diamond, Graphite.
  • They are brittle and generally soft in nature.
  • Exception: Diamond which is the hardest substances on earth.
  • They have low melting point and boiling point.
  • Exception: Diamond, Graphite, Silicon, Carbon, Boron.
  • They are not malleable in nature.

Malleability

  • Malleability is a physical property of metals that defines their ability to be hammered, pressed, or rolled into thin sheets without breaking. E.g. Similar to gold, silver is also highly malleable and can be shaped into various forms, including thin foils, and jewellery.
  • They are non-ductile in nature.

Ductility

  • Ductility is a material's ability to be stretched or drawn into a thin wire or other elongated shape without breaking, meaning it can undergo significant deformation under tensile stress. E.g. Gold, due to its high ductility, 1 gm gold can be drawn into a wire that is about 2 km long.
  • They are non-sonorous in nature.
  • They have low density.
  • Exception: Diamond.
  • They do not form Alloys.
  • Exception: Carbon is alloyed with iron to form steel.
  • They are bad conductor of heat and electricity.
  • Exception: Graphite which is a good conductor of electricity.
  • They show anionic properties.
  • Non-metals form non-metal oxides when they react with oxygen. Generally, all non-metallic oxides are acidic in nature.

Metalloids

  • Metalloids are elements that have properties of both metals and non-metals.
  • There are 7 metalloids: Boron, Silicon, Germanium, Arsenic, Antimony, Tellurium, and Polonium.

Chemical Properties of Metals

  1. 1. Reaction with Oxygen
  • Burning in air or formation of oxides (Combustion).
  • Almost all metals combine with oxygen (or air) to form metal oxides.
  • Metal + Oxygen → Metal Oxides
  • E.g. (i) 4Al + 3O₂ (g) → 2Al₂O₃ (s) (Aluminium Oxide)
  • (ii) 2Cu (s) + O₂ → 2CuO (s) (Copper Oxide)
  • Generally, metal oxides are basic in nature.

Amphoteric Oxides

  • Amphoteric oxides are compounds that can react with both acids and bases, exhibiting both acidic and basic properties, and forming salts and water in these reactions. E.g. Zinc oxide, Aluminium oxide.
  • Al₂O₃ + HCl → AlCl₃ + H₂O (Acid → Salt + Water)
  • Al₂O₃ + NaOH → NaAlO₂ + H₂O (Base → Sodium Aluminate → Salt + Water)
  • Most metal oxides are insoluble in Water.
  • Some metal oxides are soluble in water and form alkali like Sodium Oxide (Na₂O), Potassium Oxide (K₂O).

Other examples with TRICK

  • Suno: SnO (Tin oxide)
  • Be: BeO (Beryllium oxide)
  • Zanabe: ZnO (Zinc oxide)
  • Ali: Al₂O₃ (Aluminium oxide)
  • Phir: PbO₂ (Lead oxide)
  • Milenge: MnO₂ (Manganese oxide)
  • Gali matn: Ga₂O₃ (Gallium oxide)

Reactivity of Different Metals towards Oxygen

Sodium (Na) and Potassium (K)

  • These two metals react vigorously with oxygen that they catches fire if kept in open. That is why Na and K are kept in kerosene.

Mg, Al, Zn, Pb

  • At ordinary temperature, the surface of these metals gets covered with thin layer of oxides. This oxide layer protects them from further oxidation.

Iron

  • Iron does not burn on heating, but iron fillings burn vigorously when sprinkled in flame of burner.

Copper

  • Copper does not burn, but on heating, it forms a black layer of copper (II) oxide (CuO).
  • 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO
  • This black coating is responsible for tarnishing of copper objects over time.

Alkali: Those bases that dissolve in water.

Silver (Ag) and Gold (Au)

  • They do not react with oxygen even at high temperature.

Reactivity Series of Metals

(Decreasing chemical reactivity; Most reactive metal at top → Least reactive metal at bottom)

  • Potassium (K), Sodium (Na), Barium (Ba), Calcium (Ca), Magnesium (Mg), Aluminium (Al), Zinc (Zn), Iron (Fe), Nickel (Ni), Tin (Sn), Lead (Pb) — These metals are more reactive than hydrogen.
  • Hydrogen (H)
  • Copper (Cu), Mercury (Hg), Silver (Ag), Gold (Au), Platinum (Pt) — These metals are less reactive than hydrogen.

Reaction of Metal with Water

  • Metals + Water → Metal Oxide + H₂ (g)
  • All metals do not react with water
  • Metal Oxide + Water → Metal Hydroxide

Reactivity of Different Metals with Water

  • 2K (s) + 2H₂O → 2KOH (aq) + H₂ (g) + Heat
  • 2Na (s) + 2H₂O → 2NaOH (aq) + H₂ (g) + Heat
  • Ca (s) + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (aq) + H₂ (g)
  • 2Al (s) + 3H₂O → Al₂O₃ (aq) + 3H₂ (g)
  • 3Fe (s) + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ (s) + 4H₂ (g)

Reaction of Metal with Acids

  • Except a few less reactive metals (such as Cu, Hg, Ag, Au, Pt, etc.), all metals react with dilute sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) and hydrochloric acid (HCl) to produce salt and hydrogen gas.

Reaction of Metal with Dilute Nitric Acid (HNO₃)

  • Hydrogen gas is not evolved when a metal reacts with nitric acid.
  • Metal + Dilute acid → Salt + Hydrogen
  • (M) + (A) → (S) + (H)
  • Zn (s) + 2HCl (aq) → ZnCl₂ (aq) + H₂ (g)
  • This is due to strong oxidising nature of nitric acid.
  • It oxidises the hydrogen, produced to water and itself gets reduced to any of the nitrogen oxide (NO, NO₂, N₂O).
  • Magnesium (Mg) and Manganese (Mn) react with dilute HNO₃ to evolve H₂.

Dilute Solution vs Concentrated Solution

  • 1 ml acid + 4 ml water → Dilute Solution (A)
  • 4 ml acid + 1 ml water → Concentrated Solution (B)
  • Metal + HNO₃ → Salt + NO/N₂O/NO₂
  • (Exceptional case: only for Mn and Mg)
  • Metal (Mn/Mg) + HNO₃ → Salt + H₂
  • Note: Copper does not react with dilute HCl.

Aqua Regia (Royal Water)

  • It is a mixture of two strong acids in the ratio: Concentrated HNO₃ : Concentrated HCl = 1:3.
  • It is highly corrosive in nature.
  • Aqua regia is able to dissolve gold and platinum.

Reaction of Metals with solutions of other Metal Salt

  • Metal₁ + Metal₂ Salt → Metal Salt₁ + Metal (Displacement Reaction)
  • Cu (s) + 2AgNO₃ (aq) → Cu(NO₃)₂ (aq) + 2Ag (s)
  • The more reactive metal replaces the less reactive metal

Chemical Properties of Non Metals

Reaction with Oxygen

  • Non-metals do not react with water, steam or dilute acid.
  • The reason is that they act as an electron acceptor and cannot accept H⁺ ions of acids to reduce them to hydrogen gas.
  • But on heating, they readily form oxides or salts with concentrated acids.
  • S (s) + 2H₂SO₄ (conc.) →(Δ) 3SO₂ (g) + 2H₂O (l)
  • S (s) + 6HNO₃ (conc.) →(Δ) H₂SO₄ (aq) + 6NO₂ (g) + 2H₂O (aq)

Reaction between Metals and Non-metals Ionic Bond formation

Ionic Bond Formation of NaCl

  • Na configuration: 2, 8, 1; Cl configuration: 2, 8, 7
  • When Na transfers an electron to Cl, it results in NaCl. Na atom with 11 electrons and 11 proton transfers its single valence electron to Cl atom. Na becomes positively charged and Cl atom becomes negatively charged.

Electrovalent Bond

  • An electrovalent bond, also known as an ionic bond, is a chemical bond formed by the complete transfer of electrons from one atom (usually a metal) to another atom (usually a nonmetal), resulting in the formation of oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
  • Ionic compounds show anisotropic properties.

Ionic Bond Formation of MgCl₂

  • Mg²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ → Mg²⁺ 2Cl⁻ or MgCl₂

Properties of Ionic Compounds

  1. 1. Physical Nature: Ionic compounds are hard crystalline solids because of strong force of attraction between the positive and negative ions. These compounds are generally brittle and break into pieces when pressure is applied.
  2. 2. Melting and boiling points: These compounds have high melting and boiling points as large amount of energy is required to break strong inter-ionic attraction.
  3. 3. Solubility: These compounds are soluble in water (polar solvent) and insoluble in organic solvents (non-polar solvent) like kerosene, benzene, ether, petrol, etc.
  4. 4. Conduction of electricity: The conduction of electricity through a solution involves good movement of charged particle. Ionic and electrovalent compounds are good conductors of electricity, but they conduct electricity either in molten form or in their aqueous solution, as the ions are free to move and carry charge.

Occurrence of Metals in the Form of Their Ore

  • Ore has: Metal + Gangue (impurities)
  1. 1. Aluminium: Bauxite, Cryolite
  2. 2. Iron: Magnetite, Hematite, Limonite, Siderite
  3. 3. Zinc: Zinc Blende/Sphalerite; Calamine; Zincite (Zinc)
  4. 4. Mercury: Cinnabar
  5. 5. Thorium: Monazite
  6. 6. Sodium: Borax; Chile saltpeter (NaNO₃) and Indian saltpeter (KNO₃); Trona
  7. 7. Lead: Galena
  8. 8. Magnesium: Epsom salt (MgSO₄ · 7H₂O)
  9. 9. Tin: Cassiterite
  10. 10. Uranium: Pitchblende (it is made up of Uranium Oxide (UO₂) and variable proportions of UO₃)

Corrosion

  1. 1. Silver: Black coating is formed due to silver sulphide by the reaction of silver with sulphur in air and is also known as "Tarnishing of Silver".
  2. 2. Copper: Green coating due to basic copper carbonate formed by reaction of copper with carbon dioxide in air.
  3. 3. Iron: Reddish brown coating called Rust; iron corrode rapidly in air and water.

Titanium is used for making Boat because it does not corrode in sea water.

Prevention of Corrosion

  1. 1. Galvanisation: Galvanisation is protecting steel and iron from rusting by coating them with a thin layer of zinc.
  2. 2. Anodising: It is an electrochemical process that creates a thick, protective oxide layer on aluminum (and its alloys) to enhance corrosion resistance and improve its appearance.
  • Metals like aluminium, magnesium, titanium can undergo anodization to form a protective oxide layer.
  • Anodising process is used in aircraft industry.

Fact

Aluminium is more reactive than iron, yet it is less easily corroded because it forms a protective oxide layer (Al₂O₃) when exposed to oxygen.

Steps Involved in Extraction of Metals from Ores

Metallurgy

  • Metallurgy is the science of extracting metals from their ores and refining them into pure metals and alloys.
  • White gold was originally developed to imitate platinum (a naturally white metal).
  • Jewellery made of gold is an alloy. Pure gold has (22 parts of Au + 2 parts of Cu/Ag).
  • Amalgam: An amalgam is a metal alloy of mercury with one or more metal.

Extraction Flow

  • ORE → Concentration of Ore →
  • Metals of high reactivity → Electrolysis of molten ore → Pure Metal
  • Metals of medium reactivity →
  • Carbonate ore → Calcination (in absence of oxygen) → Oxide of metal → Reduction of metal → Purification of metal
  • Sulphide ore → Roasting (in presence of oxygen) → Oxide of metal → Reduction of metal
  • Metals of low reactivity → Sulphide ores → Roasting → Metal → Refining

Reduction of Metal

  • 2ZnO + C → 2Zn + CO₂ (Carbon gains oxygen / Zinc loses oxygen)

Thermite Reaction

  • It is a type of reaction in which a metal oxide is reduced by using aluminium as the reducing agent. It is generally exothermic in nature.
  • Fe₂O₃ (s) + 2Al (s) →(Δ) 2Fe (l) + Al₂O₃ (s) (Oxidation / Reduction)
  • (Iron oxide (III) / Aluminium / Iron / Aluminium oxide)
  • E.g. Railway tracks are joined using thermite reaction.

Electrolytic Refining

  • It is a process that uses electricity to purify impure metals. An impure metal is used as anode and a pure metal is used as cathode. A solution of a metal salt is used as electrolyte. When an electric current is passed through the cell, the impure metal dissolves into the electrolyte and is replaced by an equal amount of pure metal from the cathode.
  • The pure metal is deposited at the cathode, while the insoluble impurities from the impure metal settle down beneath the anode as anode mud.
